context: Original fictional illustrated teaching story; no student data.

items.text: Look at the pictures. Read or listen to the story. Choose a verb and fit it into each gap. Check your answer and use the feedback to try again. Then predict what will happen next.
The reporter looked at a photograph. Look at means direct your eyes towards something. The preposition stays after the verb.

Maya's first morning at the local news channel began with a surprise. An overnight storm had damaged the old bridge. Her editor handed her a microphone and a notebook. 'Show our viewers what happened, and check every detail,' he said. At the river, engineers were already repairing the broken railing. Maya took her first photograph. Her first report was beginning, but she did not yet know whose lives it would change.
What might Maya discover when she reaches the flooded neighbourhood?
overnight
editor
viewers
railing
notebook
Before her first assignment, Maya worked for a news channel.
The engineers worked on repairs to the bridge.

Across Greenford, families discovered the extent of the flooding through a television bulletin. Several streets were underwater. Maya's phone suddenly rang. It was Elena, her friend, calling from the community shelter. 'I'm safe,' Elena said. 'But our elderly neighbour, Mr Reed, hasn't arrived.' Maya felt relief and worry at the same time. She wrote his name in her notebook and passed the information to the rescue coordinator.
What should Maya do with information that has not yet been confirmed?
extent
bulletin
underwater
shelter
relief
The families heard about the flooding on the news.
Maya finally heard from Elena when her phone rang.

At home, a family paid close attention to a battery radio. The official instructions explained which streets were closed. Near Mr Reed's house, a firefighter raised one hand. Everyone became quiet. He turned his head towards an upstairs window, hoping to detect a faint voice. Maya stayed on the dry lane. She could see a curtain move, but she could not tell whether anyone was behind it.
What could the moving curtain mean? Suggest two possibilities.
battery
upstairs
faint
curtain
lane
The family listened to the instructions on the radio.
In complete silence, the firefighter listened for cries for help.

The rescue boat moved slowly between the houses. The crew searched each window for a sign of the missing neighbour. At the command post, two rescuers studied a map to choose a route around the fallen branches. Then a small light appeared upstairs. Mr Reed was there with his dog. Maya waited while the crew brought them to dry ground. Her notebook now contained something better than a guess: a confirmed rescue.
What might Mr Reed and his dog need when they arrive at the shelter?
crew
route
branches
missing
confirmed
Before they found Mr Reed, the rescuers looked for the missing neighbour.
To choose their route, the rescuers looked at a map.

The shelter was busy but welcoming. A parent pointed to a pile of blankets and held out her hands. Her family was cold after the journey. Mr Reed sat nearby with his dog and a cup of tea. Outside, Maya interviewed a rescue official. She wanted details of the damage, not rumours. 'Which homes are affected?' she said. The official explained what the crew had checked and what was still unknown.
Which details should Maya check before presenting her news report?
blankets
journey
damage
rumours
unknown
Because they were cold, the family asked for blankets.
During the interview, Maya asked about the damage.

By lunchtime, Maya was ready for her first broadcast. She stood on dry ground with the camera crew. She described the flood and explained how Mr Reed had reached safety. Meanwhile, new volunteers arrived at the shelter. They went straight to the coordinator, who gave them their duties. One would organise food; another would prepare beds. Maya realised that behind every headline there were people doing patient, practical work.
What other information might viewers need after this broadcast?
broadcast
headline
duties
meanwhile
safety
During her live broadcast, Maya reported on the flood.
On arrival, the volunteers reported to the shelter coordinator for instructions.

The sky darkened again. On television, a weather presenter explained that another storm was approaching. Near the shelter, a pedestrian tried to take a shortcut through a flooded street. A firefighter raised his hand and stopped her at the barrier. She returned to the dry path. Maya included the official warning in her next update. A dramatic picture was useful, but clear information could help someone make a safer decision.
How can a reporter share a warning without making an unverified claim?
approaching
shortcut
barrier
pedestrian
warning
To alert viewers to the danger, the presenter warned people about the approaching storm.
The firefighter warned people against walking through floodwater.

Inside the shelter, a nurse gently wrapped a bandage around a man's injured arm. Nearby, residents gathered around Elena as she showed a photograph of her damaged home. They listened patiently and discussed what her family would need in the coming weeks. Mr Reed's dog slept under a chair. Maya put down her microphone for a moment. The story was no longer only about water and broken buildings. It was about people who mattered to one another.
What support might families need after the immediate emergency has ended?
bandage
injured
gently
gathered
mattered
By treating their injuries, the nurse cared for injured people.
Their concern showed that the neighbours cared about the affected families.

Two days later, some homes still had no clean water. Outside their muddy houses, residents held empty containers and expressed their frustration. Elena agreed to speak for the neighbourhood. At the town hall, she presented their complaint to the mayor, together with photographs and a written request. Maya recorded the meeting. The mayor promised an update that afternoon. Maya wrote down the promise, but she knew she would need to check what happened next.
Is a promise the same as a completed action? What should Maya check next?
containers
frustration
town hall
complaint
request
The frustrated residents complained about the lack of clean water.
To present the residents’ grievance, Elena complained to the mayor.

A week later, clean water deliveries had reached the neighbourhood, and Maya checked the delivery records before sharing the update. At the community centre, students explored how rivers overflow. In another room, emergency planners reviewed photographs of crowded routes and shelters from the previous evacuation. They discussed what to improve. Mr Reed arrived with his dog and thanked the rescue crew. Maya closed her notebook. Her first assignment had taught her that a good report follows the story beyond the headline.
What did Maya learn about responsible reporting? Retell three events using the verbs from the book.
deliveries
records
overflow
crowded
beyond
During the lesson, the students learned about floods.
To improve the next evacuation, the planners learned from past mistakes.

Maya woke before sunrise. An overnight storm had damaged Greenford's old bridge, and her editor needed a reporter. Before her first assignment, Maya worked for a news channel. Her editor handed her a microphone and a notebook. 'Check every detail,' he said. Down by the river, a repair team was already busy. The engineers worked on repairs to the bridge. Maya photographed the broken railing. Her first assignment had begun, but she did not yet know whose lives it would change.

Across Greenford, television screens showed streets underwater. The families heard about the flooding on the news. Maya watched the bulletin, worried about her friend Elena. She had not received a message from her since the storm. Maya finally heard from Elena when her phone rang. 'I'm safe at the shelter,' Elena said. 'But our elderly neighbour, Mr Reed, hasn't arrived.' Maya felt relief and worry at once. She wrote his name in her notebook and called the rescue coordinator.

At home, a family sat beside a battery radio. They needed to know which streets were closed. The family listened to the instructions on the radio. Near Mr Reed's house, a firefighter raised one hand. Everyone stopped talking. In complete silence, the firefighter listened for cries for help. Maya waited on the dry lane. An upstairs curtain moved. Was someone there? She held her breath as the firefighter pointed towards the window.

The rescue boat moved slowly between the flooded houses. Mr Reed had not reached the shelter, and nobody knew where he was. The rescuers were looking for the missing neighbour. Back at the command post, two rescuers spread a street map across a table. To choose their route, the rescuers were looking at a map. They found a route around the fallen branches. Then a small light appeared upstairs. Mr Reed was there with his dog! The crew brought them safely to dry ground. Maya finally had a confirmed rescue to report.

At the shelter, a cold family stood beside a table of supplies. A parent held out her hands to a volunteer. Because they were cold, the family asked for blankets. Mr Reed sat nearby with his dog and a cup of tea. Outside, Maya opened her notebook and began questioning an official. During the interview, Maya asked about the damage. 'Which homes are affected?' she said. She wanted facts, not rumours. The official explained what the crew had checked and what was still unknown.

By lunchtime, Maya was ready to face the camera. She stood on dry ground beside the rescue boat. During her live broadcast, Maya reported on the flood. She explained how Mr Reed had reached safety. Meanwhile, new volunteers arrived, unsure where they were needed. On arrival, the volunteers reported to the shelter coordinator for instructions. One would organise food; another would prepare beds. Maya realised that behind every headline there were people doing patient, practical work.

Dark clouds returned. On television, a weather presenter pointed to the approaching storm. To alert viewers to the danger, the presenter warned people about the approaching storm. Near the shelter, a pedestrian tried to take a shortcut through a flooded street. A firefighter stopped her at the barrier. The firefighter warned people against walking through floodwater. 'Stay on the dry path,' he said. She turned back. Maya added the warning to her next update: clear information could help someone make a safer decision.

Inside the shelter, a nurse gently wrapped a bandage around a man's arm. By treating their injuries, the nurse cared for injured people. Nearby, neighbours gathered around Elena's photograph of her damaged home. They discussed how to support her family in the coming weeks. Their concern showed that the neighbours cared about the affected families. Mr Reed's dog slept under a chair. Maya put down her microphone. Her story was about much more than water and broken buildings; it was about people who mattered to one another.

Two days later, some homes still had no clean water. Residents held empty containers beside a dry tap. The frustrated residents complained about the lack of clean water. Elena agreed to speak for them. At the town hall, she placed their written complaint and photographs on the mayor's desk. To present the residents’ grievance, Elena complained to the mayor. The mayor promised an update that afternoon. Maya recorded the promise, knowing that her job was not finished. She would need to check what happened next.

A week later, clean water deliveries had reached the neighbourhood. Maya checked the delivery records before sharing the update. At the community centre, a teacher explained how rivers overflow. A good report, she now understood, follows the story beyond the headline.

Read the story together, page by page. When you reach a blank, choose between two expressions. Use the story to explain your choice. If you make a mistake, read the feedback and try again. Complete both blanks to unlock the recording. Then turn the page and continue the story.
Maya could not find her notebook. She was looking for it. Looking for means trying to find something. Looking at means directing your eyes towards something you can already see.
